Agastya's Gifts

Stories from the Ramayana

Agastya's Gifts

Ten Years of Wandering, and a Teacher's Gift

Everyday telling — Aranya Kanda, sargas 11–13

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read aloud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, the way you would sit with everyone at home and tell them a tale.

The yellow boxes are where the characters speak in their own words. Change your voice a little as you read them — Rama calm, the sage Dharmabhrita old and slow, Agastya warm and grave.

(Cues in purple) tell you when to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

At the end of every section, a green box — Pause and Think. Stop there. Ask the questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book comes from Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda, sargas 11–13. In the book before this one, Sita spoke her worry and Rama gave his answer — now the three walk on toward Agastya. Anything else you might want to know is given separately at the end, under Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — the young prince of Ayodhya. Tall, calm, kind. Warm dark-brown skin, black hair tied back, simple gold jewellery, a bow in his hand. He has already promised the sages of the forest that he will protect them.

Sita — Rama's wife, princess of Mithila. Gentle oval face, large dark eyes, warm fair wheat-gold skin, long black hair centre-parted, a single long braid with small white jasmine flowers. Small gold jhumka earrings, a thin gold nose-ring on the left nostril, gold bangles, a simple gold necklace. In the forest a simple muted green-beige saree, no crown.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother. Like Rama, but a little younger and lighter in complexion. A bow in his hand, a simple green-beige forest dress.

Dharmabhrita — a sage from Sutikshna's hermitage, who walks with the three on the road and tells them the tale of the lake. An old man with a white beard, in saffron robes.

Mandakarni — a great ascetic of long ago, who did tapas in the lake for ten thousand years.

Sutikshna — the sage of the Dandaka forest, disciple of Sharabhanga. He sent the three toward Agastya.

Agastya — the greatest sage of the Dandaka forest. Short in stature, radiant, an old man with a white beard, in saffron robes. At his word even the Vindhya mountain bowed down.

1 · The Forest Road · · THE FOREST ROAD

Taking leave of Sutikshna, the three set out again on the forest path — Rama ahead, Sita in the middle, Lakshmana behind, bow in hand.

The road was beautiful — high mountains here, dense forest there, lovely rivers in between. The three walked on, looking — the shade of the mountains, the green of the forests, the clear water of the rivers.

A sage was walking with them too — Dharmabhrita. He had come from Sutikshna's hermitage, and was showing them the way.

Walking on, the three came to a lake — and there something strange happened. From beneath the waters of the lake came the sound of music — as if some divine instrument were playing, and someone were singing.

Rama stopped. Lakshmana too stopped. Sita heard it as well — that sweet sound coming from beneath the water.

Rama asked: "O sage, what lake is this? What music is coming from beneath the water?"

Pause and think — In the middle of the forest, a lake — and from beneath its water, music! Have you ever heard a sound whose source you could not see? And when something strange appears, what should we do — run away in fear, or stop and ask? Rama stopped and asked.

2 · The Lake of the Five Apsaras · · THE LAKE OF THE FIVE APSARAS

The sage Dharmabhrita smiled and said — "Rama, this lake is called the Lake of the Five Apsaras. The sage Mandakarni built it by the power of his tapas."

"Mandakarni was a great ascetic. He stood in the waters of this lake and did fierce tapas for ten thousand years — living on air alone, and nothing else."

"Seeing his tapas, the gods grew worried. With Agni, the fire-god, at their head, they met together — and sent five apsaras, whose shine was like lightning, to break Mandakarni's tapas."

Dharmabhrita said: "And those five apsaras led Mandakarni away with them — they built a house beneath the waters, and Mandakarni lives there with them to this day. The music you hear comes from that house."

The three looked at the lake — and heard its tale. Then they walked on — going from hermitage to hermitage, meeting the sages.

And in this way — wandering among the hermitages, meeting the sages — ten years passed.

Pause and think — Mandakarni did tapas for ten thousand years — and then went to live with the five apsaras. The gods sent the apsaras to break his tapas. Is it right to break someone's tapas? And ten years — spent wandering among the hermitages — is that a very long time, or does time pass just like that in the forest?

3 · Ten Years, and Back to Sutikshna · · TEN YEARS, AND BACK TO SUTIKSHNA

Ten years passed — living in the hermitages of the Dandaka forest, meeting the sages, living in the peace of the forest.

Then one day the three came back again to the hermitage of the sage Sutikshna. Sutikshna welcomed them — and the three stayed there for a while.

Then Rama said to Sutikshna — "Gurudev, now we wish to see the sage Agastya. You said he is the greatest sage of the Dandaka forest."

Sutikshna said: "Rama, go four yojanas to the south from here — there is the hermitage of Agastya's brother. Then go one yojana further south — at the edge of the forest you will find Agastya's hermitage."

"And listen, Rama — Agastya is the sage at whose word Mount Vindhya stopped growing, so that it would not block the path of the sun. There is no measure to his tapas or his age — gods, gandharvas, siddhas and sages all worship him."

The three touched Sutikshna's feet, and set out toward Agastya.

Pause and think — Ten years passed — and Rama asked Sutikshna again about Agastya. Does learning take such a long time? And does a teacher send his disciple on to the next teacher — as Sutikshna sent Rama to Agastya?

4 · How the Vindhya Bowed · · HOW THE VINDHYA BOWED

On the road, Rama began to tell Lakshmana of Agastya's greatness — "Lakshmana, listen — how great Agastya is."

"Long ago the Vindhya mountain began to grow — taller, and taller, and taller. It grew so tall that it began to block the path of the sun. The sun could not move across the sky — and darkness began to fall over the world."

"Then Agastya went to the Vindhya — and said to it — 'Vindhya, bow down. Stay bowed until I return.'"

Rama said: "And the Vindhya bowed down, Lakshmana. Agastya went away to the south — and never returned. That is why the Vindhya is bowed down even today — and the sun's path is open."

Lakshmana heard this — and his respect for Agastya grew even greater. "Brother," he said, "seeing such a sage is a blessing indeed."

And the three walked on — past the hermitage of Agastya's brother, then one yojana further — toward the hermitage of Agastya.

Pause and think — Mount Vindhya obeyed Agastya's word — and bowed down. Can a mountain obey someone's word? And Agastya said to the Vindhya — stay bowed until I return — and he never returned. Was that a trick — or did the Vindhya itself accept to stay bowed?

5 · Agastya's Hermitage · · AGASTYA'S HERMITAGE

Coming near Agastya's hermitage, Lakshmana went ahead — and said to a disciple standing at the gate — "Rama, the son of Dasharatha, has come with his wife Sita, and wishes to see the sage Agastya. I am his younger brother Lakshmana."

The disciple heard this — and ran to tell Agastya. Hearing it, Agastya was filled with joy.

Agastya said: "What! Rama has come! This is my good fortune — I have waited years to see him. Why did you not bring them in at once? Why this delay?"

Rama waited outside — and saw the peace of the hermitage. Birds roamed there in freedom, and sang. Altars stood there for Brahma, Vishnu, Maheshwara, Indra, Kubera, Dhatri, Vidhatri, Gayatri, the Sun, the Moon, the serpent Sesha, and the Vasus.

Then Agastya himself came out of the hermitage — to meet his honoured guests. Rama saw him — and said to Lakshmana — "This radiance can belong to none but Agastya."

The three bowed at Agastya's feet. Agastya raised them with great love — and embraced them.

Pause and think — Agastya said — why did you not bring them in at once? Why this delay? Is such eagerness good, when a great guest arrives? And Rama saw so much peace in the hermitage — is peace itself the mark of a place?

6 · The Divine Weapons · · THE DIVINE WEAPONS

Agastya welcomed Rama — with great love and affection.

Agastya said: "Rama, you are the king of all the worlds, unfailing in dharma, and worthy of worship. You have come as my beloved guest — this is my good fortune. Now I give you the bow of Vishnu."

Agastya showed Rama the Vaishnava bow — of gold, encrusted with gems, crafted by Vishwakarma. With this very bow Vishnu had slain great asuras — and restored the lustre of heaven.

"And take these arrows, Rama — shining like the sun, burning like fire. And these two quivers — in which the arrows never run out — Indra gave them to me."

"And take this sword — whose hilt and sheath are of burnished gold. This is the sword of Brahmadatta — with which Vishnu vanquished the rakshasas."

Agastya said: "Rama, take all of these — and win victory as Indra did with the vajra."

Rama received the divine weapons with folded hands — the bow, the arrows, the two quivers, and the sword.

Pause and think — Agastya gave Rama the weapons he had kept with care for years — Vishnu's bow, Indra's quivers, Brahmadatta's sword. Does a teacher give his disciple his most precious thing? And is receiving weapons enough — or must one also learn to wield them?

7 · Towards Panchavati · · TOWARDS PANCHAVATI

Then Rama asked Agastya — "Gurudev, now tell me — where should we live? Which place in the forest would be good for us to stay?"

Agastya said — "Rama, ahead there is a place — Panchavati. It lies on the banks of the Godavari river — full of fruits, roots and water, holy and pleasant. Sages live there — and the place is blessed."

Agastya said: "Rama, live in Panchavati with Lakshmana and Sita — that place is right for you."

Rama heard this — and agreed at once. He touched Agastya's feet — and the three set out for Panchavati.

The road was clear — and the three walked on firmly, without fear, toward Panchavati — where their next story was about to begin.

Pause and think — Agastya gave Rama weapons — and then he also told him where to live. Does a teacher only teach — or does he also give a place to live? And Panchavati — full of fruits, roots and water — is that what matters most in a place to live?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

There are three tales in this story — a lake that makes music; a mountain that bowed down; and a sage who gave Rama divine weapons.

Mandakarni did tapas for ten thousand years — and then went to live with the apsaras. The Vindhya obeyed Agastya's word — and bowed down. And Agastya gave Rama the weapons he had kept with care for years.

Ask the listeners:

1. Music was coming from beneath the waters of the lake — and Rama stopped and asked. When something strange appears, what should we do — run away in fear, or stop and ask?

2. Mandakarni did tapas for ten thousand years — and then went to live with the five apsaras. The gods had sent the apsaras to break his tapas. Is it right to break someone's tapas?

3. Ten years passed — wandering among the hermitages. Does learning take such a long time?

4. Mount Vindhya obeyed Agastya's word — and bowed down. Can a mountain obey someone's word?

5. Agastya gave Rama the weapons he had kept with care for years. Does a teacher give his disciple his most precious thing?

6. Agastya also told Rama where to live — Panchavati. Does a teacher only teach — or does he also give a place to live?

7. Sutikshna sent Rama to Agastya — as one teacher sends his disciple to the next teacher. Does learning ever end?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main source

The main story of this book is from Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda, sargas 11–13 — the Lake of the Five Apsaras, the ten years of wandering, the meeting with Agastya, the divine weapons, and the departure for Panchavati.

The Lake of the Five Apsaras — Sarga 11

The divine music heard from beneath the waters of the lake, the sage Dharmabhrita telling Mandakarni's tale, Mandakarni doing tapas for ten thousand years in the lake living on air alone, the gods growing worried and sending five apsaras, and Mandakarni building a house beneath the waters and living there with them — is in sarga 11.

The ten years — Sarga 11

The ten years passing as they wander among the hermitages after the lake, the return to Sutikshna's hermitage, staying there a while, and Sutikshna directing them onward — four yojanas south to the hermitage of Agastya's brother, then one yojana further to Agastya's — is in sarga 11.

The Vindhya bows — Sarga 11

Rama telling Lakshmana on the road of Agastya's greatness — the Vindhya mountain growing tall and blocking the sun's path, Agastya telling it to bow down, and the Vindhya staying bowed — is in sarga 11.

Meeting Agastya — Sarga 12

Lakshmana telling the disciple at the gate of Rama's arrival, Agastya's joyful words — "Why did you not bring them in at once?" — Rama seeing the peace of the hermitage and the altars of the gods, Agastya coming out to meet them, and the three bowing before him — is in sarga 12.

The divine weapons — Sarga 12

The Vaishnava bow — gold, gem-encrusted, made by Vishwakarma, with which Vishnu slew great asuras — the shining arrows, the two inexhaustible quivers given by Indra, and the sword of Brahmadatta in its golden sheath — and Agastya's words — "Win victory as Indra did" — are in sarga 12.

Panchavati — Sarga 13

Rama asking where he should live, Agastya naming Panchavati — on the Godavari, full of fruits, roots and water, a holy place — Rama agreeing, and the three setting out for Panchavati — is in sarga 13.

Agastya's other famous deeds

Agastya's other famous deeds — drinking the ocean, and slaying Vatapi and Ilvala — are not told in these sargas; they come at other places in the Ramayana and other texts. That is why they are not in the main story of this book.

What happens next

On the road to Panchavati the three meet Jatayu — that story is in the next book of this series.

The End · · THE END

Here the story of the meeting with Agastya rests — a lake that makes music, a mountain that bowed down, and a sage who gave Rama divine weapons and showed him the road to Panchavati.

And whenever something strange appears before you, remember Rama — who stopped and asked. And whenever someone asks you for something, remember Agastya — who gave away his most precious thing.

‖ The End ‖
